title: What a wave knows about the wind
teaches: Waves carry energy, not water; fetch and duration, chop and swell, wave speed in deep and shallow water, and waves against a current
summary: **A wave carries energy, not water.** Each bit of water goes round a small loop as a wave passes and ends up nearly where it started.
**The motion fades with depth.** Half a wavelength down, the loops are about a twentieth the size of those at the surface, so the water below a storm is still.
**In deep water, the period sets the speed.** A wave travels about 1.56 m/s for each second of its period, so long waves outrun short ones.

**Three things cap a wind's waves.** The fetch (how much open water the wind blows over), the duration, and the point where the waves travel as fast as the wind; whichever comes first sets their size.
**Chop is young and swell is old.** Chop is short, steep waves still under their wind; swell is long, smooth waves that have left their storm behind.
**In shallow water, the depth sets the speed.** Where a wave is more than twenty times as long as the water is deep, it travels at √(g × depth), whatever its period.
**A current running against waves steepens them.** On the ebb, the falling tide, the outflow off Point Wilson shortens incoming waves until they break.
**A fast boat makes long waves.** The longest waves of its wake travel at the boat's own speed, so their period is as long as ocean swell's, and they come ashore hard.

blocks.text: On 8 January 1904 the steamer *Clallam* left Seattle for Victoria, on the southern tip of Vancouver Island. She was a wooden passenger steamer, built the year before at Tacoma, and she called on the way at Port Townsend, near Point Wilson, where Puget Sound's northern entrance, Admiralty Inlet, opens into the Strait of Juan de Fuca. The Strait runs about 150 km west from there to the open Pacific, between the Olympic Peninsula and Vancouver Island. Past Point Wilson the *Clallam* turned out into it, into a winter gale.

Out in the Strait she began to take on water faster than her pumps could clear it, and the water rose until it put out the fires under her boilers. Without steam she could not keep her bow to the seas, and lay rolling broadside to them. Her officers put the women and children into the lifeboats. The boats were swamped or overturned close to the ship, and none of the women and children in them survived. The *Clallam* stayed afloat into the night, taken in tow by a tug, and sank before she reached shelter. More than fifty people died.[^clallam]

blocks.caption: The *Clallam*'s route ran north up Puget Sound to Point Wilson, then northwest across the Strait to Victoria. The dashed green lines show how much open water a wind has along the main basin of the Sound and along the Strait; the blue arcs are swell rolling in from the Pacific.

key.text: Fetch for a wind along the water

blocks.text: A ferry passenger sees a milder version of the same contrast. A breezy day on the Seattle to Bainbridge run brings short, choppy waves with white tops, while the Port Townsend to Coupeville crossing, at the inner end of the Strait, is cancelled now and then for rough water. The wind can be the same on both. This lesson's puzzle is what a wind needs, besides strength, to raise big waves, and why the Strait has it and the Sound does not.

Watch a gull or a drifting log on the Sound as waves pass under it. It rises on each high point of a wave, its **crest**, slides a little forward, drops into the low point between crests, the **trough**, slides a little back, and after a minute it is close to where it started. The wave has gone on toward the shore; the water it travelled through has not.

**A common misconception** is that waves carry water to the beach. If they did, a day of waves rolling onto Alki would pile the Sound up against the shore. What travels is the shape of the wave and the energy that holds it up. Under a passing wave each small parcel of water goes round a loop, up and forward under the crest, down and back under the trough, and comes home as the next crest arrives.

Three numbers describe a wave. Its **period** is the time between one crest and the next passing a fixed post, which is also the time each parcel takes to go round its loop. Its **wavelength** is the distance from crest to crest. Its **height** is the drop from crest to trough.

The loops shrink with depth. Half a wavelength down they are about a twentieth the size of those at the surface, and a whole wavelength down they are tiny. In water deeper than about half a wavelength, a wave knows nothing of the bottom. A submarine a hundred metres down rides out a storm in nearly still water, and the waves the wind raises on the Sound itself, a few tens of metres long at most, never reach the floor of its main basin, mostly more than 100 m down.

blocks.caption: Water parcels (dots) under a passing wave, each going round its own loop, and a bottle floating on the surface. Two sliders set the wave's period and the water's depth. The drawing is always one and a third wavelengths across. Up and down are drawn larger than true, so the loops can be seen. A model of small waves.
blocks.task: Raise the sea floor (less depth) until the loops near the bottom flatten and the floor appears

blocks.text: The bottle goes round with the water and is barely carried along.[^drift] What the wave hands on, from each parcel to the next, is energy: the wind's work, stored as water lifted against gravity and water set moving. That energy can cross an ocean, as the next part shows. A storm off Japan can raise waves that break on the Washington coast a week or more later, delivered by water that never left the western Pacific.

In deep water a wave's speed depends on its period and on nothing else. It travels about **1.56 metres a second for each second of period**, a number that comes from gravity: 1.56 is the 9.8 m/s² of the Earth's pull, written g, divided by 2π.[^dispersion] A crest moves one wavelength in one period, so the wavelength is the speed times the period: 1.56 × period × period, in metres. A 3-second chop on the Sound moves at under 5 m/s, with crests 14 m apart. A 12-second swell off La Push, on the outer coast, moves at 19 m/s, about 67 km/h, with crests 225 m apart.

blocks.caption: Crest to crest in deep water, from the period alone: wavelength = 1.56 × period², in metres.

options.title: How far apart the crests are

blocks.text: Because long waves outrun short ones, a distant storm sorts its own waves: the long ones arrive first, and the shorter ones follow over the next days. One more fact matters for how fast they arrive. Waves at sea travel in groups, and in deep water a group, with the energy in it, moves at half the speed of its crests. Watch a group closely and each crest seems to appear at its back, run forward through it, and die at its front. A crest is a shape; the energy is what arrives.

**Estimate.** A storm in the Gulf of Alaska, about 2,000 km from Cape Flattery, sends out a swell with a 14-second period. Its crests travel at 1.56 × 14, about 22 m/s, and its energy at half that, about 11 m/s. 2,000 km at 11 m/s is about 180,000 seconds: two days. An 8-second swell from the same storm, its energy moving at about 6 m/s, takes nearly four days.

**Out in the field.** From a pier or a beach, pick a fixed post or a buoy and count the seconds while eleven crests pass it: that is ten periods. On a breezy afternoon off Alki the answer is usually 20 to 30 seconds, chop of 2 or 3 seconds. On the outer coast at Rialto Beach or Kalaloch it is often 100 seconds or more, swell of 10 seconds or longer.

Wind blowing over flat water roughens it into ripples, and the ripples give the wind something to push against. The push builds them into waves, and bigger, longer waves take more from the wind. Three things stop that growth.

The waves can run out of room. The **fetch** is the distance of open water the wind blows over, and a wave that reaches the far shore stops growing. They can run out of time: the **duration** is how long the wind has blown, and young waves need hours to grow across a long fetch: under a 30-knot wind, about four hours to grow across 40 km of water, and about ten across 150 km. And they can catch the wind. The wind pushes on a wave only by blowing faster than it moves, against its back; once the longest waves travel nearly as fast as the wind, it has nothing left to push on, and the sea is **fully developed**. That takes a lot of room. Under a 30-knot wind (15 m/s) it takes about 500 km of fetch and a day of steady wind, and the waves reach about 6 m (19 feet) with an 11-second period: open-ocean waves.[^sverdrup]
The heights here are what a forecast calls the **significant height**, the average of the highest third of the waves.[^height] The figure asks a question you can answer from the last paragraph.

blocks.caption: The waves a steady wind raises. Three sliders set the wind speed, the fetch and the duration. Under the waves, three bars give the height each limit alone would allow, on a scale where each step is ten times the last; the shortest bar is the one that applies. A model: a growth law fitted to measurements of waves in the North Sea.
blocks.task: Guess, then find a setting where each of the three is the limit

blocks.text: On the Sound it is nearly always the fetch. A 30-knot southerly blowing up the main basin has 40 km or so of open water to work with, and however long it blows, the waves stop at about 1.6 m (5 feet) with a period near 5 seconds. Across a 10 km reach of the Sound they get under a metre and about 3 seconds. Lake Washington, long and narrow, raises the same kind of short, steep chop in a north or south gale.

The Strait gives a wind blowing along it about 150 km. The same 30 knots, blowing for twelve hours, raise waves about 3 m (10 feet) high with a period of 8 seconds, twice the height for the same wind, and here the fetch is still the limit. If the gale has blown for only six hours, it is the duration: the waves have not yet grown all the way down the Strait, and stand at about 2 m. Even 150 km is far short of the 500 km a 30-knot sea needs to develop fully, so the biggest waves in the Strait come in from outside.

Waves still under the wind that is making them are **chop**, or a wind sea: short, steep, uneven, a mix of periods and directions, with whitecaps where the wind tears the crests. Once waves leave their wind behind, by outrunning the storm or by the storm moving on, the short ones die out and the long ones go on as **swell**: smooth, long-crested waves that come in at a steady beat.

Puget Sound is almost all chop. It is closed off from the ocean by the Olympic Peninsula and Vancouver Island, and its waves are raised by the local wind over a few tens of kilometres. The western Strait is different. Swell from the open Pacific rolls in at its mouth, as the map in the first part shows, and a boat off Neah Bay, just inside Cape Flattery, can meet a long ocean swell from one direction with a steep local chop on top of it from another, two seas from two winds at once. Two sets of waves passing through each other add: where a crest of one meets a crest of the other, the water stands as high as both together. Farther east the swell spreads out into the widening Strait and fades, and little of it gets past Point Wilson into the Sound.

Twice a day the tide falls, and while it falls the water runs out of Puget Sound through Admiralty Inlet and past Point Wilson into the Strait: the **ebb**. While the tide rises, the water runs back in: the **flood**. Between them, as the current turns, comes **slack water**, when the current stops. (Lessons 8 to 11 explain the tide and these currents.) On summer afternoons a **westerly**, a wind from the west, blows in from the ocean along the Strait, and the waves it raises run east, straight into the outgoing ebb.

A wave meeting a current keeps its period, since its crests still arrive at a buoy as often as before. But it has to make headway against moving water, so it covers less ground in each period: its crests bunch closer together. Its energy bunches up too. Energy keeps arriving from the west at the same rate, but against the current it makes slower progress, so it piles up, as cars pile up where traffic slows; more energy in each metre of sea means taller waves. Height over length is a wave's **steepness**, and once a wave's height passes about a seventh of its length the crest can no longer hold its shape and topples.

In the model the figure uses, a 4-second wave's energy travels at about 3 m/s, and a current of about 3 knots (1.5 m/s) against it would stop its energy making headway at all. The waves break before that point.

blocks.caption: A 4-second wind sea running east into an ebb that runs west, as off Point Wilson on an afternoon westerly. The slider sets the speed of the ebb. Across, 100 m to scale; up and down, four times true. A model of deep-water waves on a steady current.
blocks.task: Guess, then speed up the ebb until the waves break

blocks.text: Two or three knots is enough, and the ebb off Point Wilson often runs that fast. The result is a **tide rip**: a band of short, steep, breaking seas, often with a clear edge where the current begins, standing in the same place while the waves rush through it. Small boats plan their crossings of the eastern Strait around it, going at slack water or when the current runs the same way as the waves. The same trouble, on a bigger scale, meets ships where the Columbia River's outflow runs into Pacific swell, the subject of a lesson in the Columbia branch.

parts.title: Shallow water, and the wakes in Rich Passage

blocks.text: When a wave moves into water shallower than half its wavelength, its loops reach the bottom and are flattened against it, and the wave slows. Once the wave is more than twenty times as long as the water is deep, its period no longer matters at all: **a wave in shallow water travels at the square root of g times the depth**, √(g h), where h is the depth in metres. In water 1 m deep that is 3.1 m/s; in 2 m, 4.4 m/s; in 5 m, 7 m/s. Between the two limits, from half a wavelength deep down to a twentieth, the speed lies between the deep-water rule and the shallow-water rule, closer to the shallow rule the shallower it gets.

blocks.caption: The same wave, now in shallower water. A longer period means a longer wave, which feels the bottom sooner. Shallow water is drawn deeper than true, so its loops can be seen.
blocks.task: Make the water shallow for the wave

blocks.text: A wave keeps its period as it comes into shallow water: crests arrive at the beach as often as they passed the buoy offshore. What changes is its speed, and with it its length. As the depth falls the wave slows, its crests crowd together and its height grows, much as against a current, until the wave is about as high as the water is deep, and it breaks. Long waves feel the bottom long before short ones: a 3-second chop behaves as a deep-water wave anywhere deeper than 7 m, while a 14-second swell starts to feel the bottom 150 m down. Lesson 10 takes this to the longest wave in the Sound, the tide, which is hundreds of kilometres long, so that even the deepest water in the Sound is shallow for it: in 100 m of water it travels at √(9.8 × 100), about 31 m/s.

Rich Passage is the narrow, winding channel between Bainbridge Island and the Kitsap Peninsula, through which the Seattle to Bremerton ferries run. In the late 1990s the state put fast passenger ferries on that run, travelling at over 30 knots. Owners of beaches along the passage soon said the wakes were stripping sand and gravel from their shores and undermining their bulkheads, and took the state to court. The fast boats were made to slow down through the passage, which took away most of the time they saved. Kitsap Transit spent years in the 2010s testing a hull shaped to make a small wake at speed, and since 2017 its fast ferries, built to that kind of design, have run through the passage at speed again.[^wake]

A wake did damage that storms had not because of period. A boat's wake is a set of waves its hull keeps making, and the longest of them have crests that keep pace with the boat. In deep water a wave whose crests move at 30 knots, about 15 m/s, has a period of about 15 / 1.56, nearly 10 seconds: a swell, in a passage sheltered from everything but local chop of 2 or 3 seconds. Out in the channel such waves are low and easy to miss. They keep their period as they reach the shallows, where they slow, steepen and come ashore with far more energy than the chop the beaches had been shaped by, every time a boat went by.

blocks.caption: Six questions on waves
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A bottle floats in deep water beyond the surf while ten waves of swell pass under it. Where does it end up?
choices: Close to where it started, having gone round a small loop with each wave
About ten wavelengths nearer the shore, carried one wavelength by each crest
A little farther out to sea, drawn back under each trough more than it goes forward
items.why: A wave carries energy, not water. Each parcel of water, and anything floating on it, goes round a loop as a wave passes and comes back nearly to where it began; only a slow drift carries it forward.

items.ask: A steady 30-knot wind has blown for two days along a lake 5 km long. Which change would raise the biggest waves?
choices: A longer lake, with more open water downwind
Another day of the same wind on the same lake
Deeper water in the same lake, under the same wind
items.why: On a 5 km lake the fetch is the limit: the waves reach the far shore long before two days are up. More time adds nothing, and these short waves never feel the bottom, so only more fetch helps.

items.ask: In the same 30-knot gale, why is the Strait of Juan de Fuca often far rougher than Puget Sound?
choices: The wind has far more open water there, and swell comes in from the Pacific
Gales there last longer, so the waves have more time to grow at the same fetch
Its deeper water lets the waves grow taller before they feel the bottom
items.why: On the Sound a 30-knot wind's waves are capped by a fetch of a few tens of kilometres. The Strait gives it about 150 km, and Pacific swell adds a second sea.

items.ask: Wind waves running east off Point Wilson turn short, steep and breaking when the ebb begins. Why?
choices: The ebb runs against them, so they shorten and their energy piles into taller crests
The ebb lowers the water off the point, so the waves feel the bottom and break
The ebb runs with the wind, so the wind builds the waves faster than before
items.why: A wave meeting a current keeps its period but makes less headway, so its crests bunch together and its energy piles up. Past a steepness of about one in seven, it breaks.

items.ask: A swell with a 12-second period crosses a shoal 2 m deep. What sets its speed there?
choices: The wind: about the speed of the wind that raised it
items.why: At 4.4 m/s a 12-second wave is about 53 m long, more than twenty times the depth, so the water is shallow for it and its speed is √(g h). The deep-water rule no longer applies.

items.ask: Why did fast ferries' wakes wear away beaches in Rich Passage that storms had left alone?
choices: The longest wake waves had periods near 10 seconds and steepened hard in the shallows
The wakes were steep chop of 2 or 3 seconds, steeper than any storm waves there
The wakes came so often that sand had no time to settle back between them
items.why: The longest waves of a wake keep pace with the boat, so at 30 knots their period is about 10 seconds, like swell. Low in the channel, they slow and steepen in shallow water and carry far more energy ashore than local chop.

clallam.title: How many died
clallam.text: Accounts of the *Clallam*'s loss give slightly different totals for the dead, most of them in the mid fifties. It remains one of the worst losses of life on these waters.

height.title: Significant height
height.text: A real sea is a jumble of waves of different sizes. Forecasts and buoys give the significant wave height because it is close to what an experienced sailor would call the height by eye. Among a few thousand waves, one may be nearly twice the significant height.

drift.title: A slow drift
drift.text: The loops do not quite close: a parcel moves a little farther forward under the crest than it comes back under the trough, so floating things creep along in the direction the waves travel. This **Stokes drift**, named after George Stokes, who worked it out in 1847, is a few centimetres a second for ordinary waves. The wind's drag on the surface adds a little more.

dispersion.title: One formula for every depth
dispersion.text: A wave of wavelength L in water h deep travels at a speed c = √((g L / 2π) × tanh(2π h / L)), where tanh is a function that is nearly 1 for large numbers and nearly equal to its input for small ones. In deep water it is 1, and c = √(g L / 2π); since L = c T for a period T, this works out to c = g T / 2π, the 1.56 m/s per second of period. In shallow water tanh(x) is nearly x, and c = √(g h).

sverdrup.title: Forecasting surf for a landing
sverdrup.text: The first practical rules for wave height from wind speed, fetch and duration were worked out during the Second World War by Harald Sverdrup and Walter Munk at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, to forecast the surf on beaches before Allied landings, among them Normandy in June 1944. Later measurement campaigns, above all the Joint North Sea Wave Project of 1968 and 1969, refined them into laws like the one the figure uses.

wake.title: A wake in shallow water
wake.text: A boat makes two sets of waves: a fan of short waves spreading out at an angle on each side, and waves across its track that follow it at its own speed. In shallow water no wave can go faster than √(g h), and a boat moving at close to that speed piles its wake up into much larger, longer waves; fast ferries are designed to pass through that speed quickly or avoid it.
